title: Dedekind Domains and the Failure of Unique Element Factorization in ℤ[√-5]
description: Proves that Dedekind domains generalize unique factorization from elements to ideals, while demonstrating that element-level factorization can fail. The classic example ℤ[√-5] is a Dedekind domain where 6 = 2·3 = (1+√-5)(1-√-5) gives two distinct irreducible factorizations. The element 2 is proved irreducible (norm analysis: N = 2 or 3 are impossible) but not prime (N(2) = 4 does not divide N(1±√-5) = 6), so ℤ[√-5] is not a UFD despite being a Dedekind domain. Proves: PID → Dedekind, prime ideals = maximal ideals in Dedekind domains, norm multiplicativity, and the unit characterization N = 1.

sections.title: Imports and Setup
sections.summary: Imports Mathlib and the parent Bezout/UFD chain file. Module header describes Dedekind domains, ideal unique factorization, and the ℤ[√-5] counterexample. Defines the ZSqrtNeg5 abbreviation for ℤ[√-5] = Zsqrtd(-5).
sections.mathContext: Dedekind domains satisfy: every nonzero prime ideal is maximal (Krull dimension ≤ 1). The ideal FTA states every nonzero proper ideal factors uniquely into prime ideals — the right generalization of the FTA from elements to ideals.

sections.title: Dedekind Domain Instances
sections.summary: Establishes that ℤ and k[x] (polynomial ring over a field) are Dedekind domains via inference. Proves pid_is_dedekind: every PID is a Dedekind domain. Proves prime_ideal_is_maximal via IsDedekindDomain.dimensionLtOne.
sections.mathContext: The hierarchy EuclideanDomain → PID → Dedekind domain → IntegralDomain holds. The characterization of Dedekind domains by Krull dimension forces every nonzero prime ideal to be maximal.

sections.title: Norm Theory for ℤ[√-5]
sections.summary: Proves norm_formula (N(a+b√-5) = a²+5b²), norm_nonneg, norm_mul_eq (multiplicativity), and norm computations for the four factors: N(2)=4, N(3)=9, N(1±√-5)=6. Private lemmas show N=2 and N=3 have no solutions by bounding b and using interval_cases on re.
sections.mathContext: The norm N: ℤ[√d] → ℤ sends a+b√d ↦ a²-db². For d=-5 this gives N = a²+5b² ≥ 0. Multiplicativity N(αβ) = N(α)N(β) is the key tool for factorization proofs. Elements with N=1 are exactly the units.

sections.title: Unit Characterization
sections.summary: Proves isUnit_iff_norm_one: z is a unit in ℤ[√-5] iff N(z) = 1. Forward direction: N(z)·N(z⁻¹) = 1 with nonnegativity forces N(z) = 1. Backward direction: if N(z) = 1, then z·conj(z) = ⟨N(z),0⟩ = 1 exhibits an explicit inverse. Proves two_not_unit from N(2) = 4 ≠ 1.
sections.mathContext: Units of ℤ[√d] with d < 0 have norm 1; for d = -5, the only units are ±1 (N = 1 forces a = ±1, b = 0 from a²+5b² = 1). The conjugate z* = a-b√-5 gives the inverse when N(z) = 1.

sections.title: Irreducibility vs. Primality of 2
sections.summary: Proves two_irreducible: if 2 = a·b then N(a)·N(b) = 4, and since N=2 and N=3 are impossible, exactly one of N(a)=1 or N(b)=1. Proves two_not_prime: 2 | (1+√-5)(1-√-5) = 6 but 2 ∤ (1±√-5) because N(2)=4 ∤ N(1±√-5)=6, giving a norm divisibility contradiction.
sections.mathContext: Irreducible means non-unit with no non-trivial factorization. Prime means: p|ab implies p|a or p|b. In a UFD these coincide; in ℤ[√-5] they diverge: 2 is irreducible (norm forces factor to be a unit) but not prime (fails to divide either factor of its product).

sections.title: Non-UFD Conclusion and Structural Results
sections.summary: Proves zsqrtneg5_not_ufd: in a UFD irreducible implies prime (UniqueFactorizationMonoid.irreducible_iff_prime), so two_irreducible + two_not_prime contradicts UFD status. Proves irred_imp_prime_in_ufd, hierarchy (PID → Dedekind ∧ UFD), and zsqrtneg5_witness bundling all three facts.
sections.mathContext: The theorem that UFDs have irreducible = prime is Mathlib's UniqueFactorizationMonoid.irreducible_iff_prime. The key implication: Dedekind domain is a UFD iff it is a PID. Since ℤ[√-5] is not a UFD, it is not a PID — its ideal class group has order 2, generated by the ideal (2, 1+√-5).

overview.historicalContext: Richard Dedekind introduced Dedekind domains in 1871 while studying algebraic integers and developing ideal theory. His key insight was that while element-level unique factorization fails in rings like ℤ[√-5], it is restored at the level of ideals. The example ℤ[√-5] with its dual factorization 6 = 2·3 = (1+√-5)(1-√-5) — recognized by Kummer and Dedekind — was the historical impetus for ideal theory. Ernst Kummer had earlier introduced 'ideal numbers' to restore unique factorization, and Dedekind reformulated this rigorously as ideals in 1871. This formalization proves the essential classical facts: 2 is irreducible but not prime, ℤ[√-5] fails to be a UFD, and Dedekind domains are exactly the right setting where ideal unique factorization holds.
overview.problemStatement: Let $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ denote the ring of algebraic integers $\{a+b\sqrt{-5} : a, b \in \mathbb{Z}\}$ with norm $N(a+b\sqrt{-5}) = a^2+5b^2$. The dual factorization $6 = 2 \cdot 3 = (1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$ shows element-level unique factorization fails. Prove: (1) 2 is irreducible (any factorization $2 = ab$ has $N(a) \in \{1,4\}$, so $a$ or $b$ is a unit); (2) 2 is not prime ($2 \mid (1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$ but $4 \nmid 6$); (3) $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ is not a UFD.
overview.proofStrategy: The proof has four phases: (1) Dedekind instances — establish ℤ and k[x] as Dedekind domains by typeclass inference, and prove prime_ideal_is_maximal via IsDedekindDomain.dimensionLtOne. (2) Norm theory — prove N(a+b√-5)=a²+5b²  is multiplicative and compute N for the four factors of 6. (3) Norm gap — prove a²+5b²≠2 and ≠3 by bounding b=0 with nlinarith and exhausting a∈{-1,0,1} with interval_cases. (4) Divergence — from the norm gap, any factorization 2=ab has N(a)∈{1,4}, proving irreducibility; the equation 6=4·N(k) has no solution, proving non-primality; UniqueFactorizationMonoid.irreducible_iff_prime then gives a contradiction with UFD.
keyInsights: The norm gap — a²+5b² ≠ 2 and ≠ 3 for any integers a, b — is the arithmetic heart of the proof. This gap exists because 2 is not a quadratic residue mod 5, making the prime 2 ramify as (2,1+√-5)² rather than split in ℤ[√-5].

The norm divisibility criterion converts element divisibility questions into integer arithmetic: α ∤ β iff N(α) ∤ N(β). Since N(2)=4 and N(1±√-5)=6, and 4 ∤ 6, we get 2 ∤ (1±√-5) — no Lean divisibility search needed.

Mathlib's UniqueFactorizationMonoid.irreducible_iff_prime is the bridge between the element-level properties and the UFD conclusion: it converts the two properties (irreducible, not prime) into a direct contradiction with any UFD instance.

The Lean proof uses decide for the dual factorization 2·3 = (1+√-5)(1-√-5) and norm computations, reducing concrete arithmetic in ℤ[√-5] to kernel computation. This demonstrates the power of decidability in formal mathematics.

The ideal class group Cl(ℤ[√-5]) ≅ ℤ/2ℤ is the algebraic invariant behind this failure: the non-principal ideal (2,1+√-5) has class of order 2, and the two element factorizations of 6 correspond to the two ways of decomposing the principal ideal (6) = p₁²·p₂·p₃ into prime ideal products.

conclusion.summary: The file proves 18 theorems with 0 sorries and 0 axioms, fully machine-checked. Key results: 2 is irreducible in ℤ[√-5] (norm analysis closes all factorization cases); 2 is not prime (norm divisibility 4 ∤ 6 gives contradiction); ℤ[√-5] is not a UFD (irreducible ≠ prime via UniqueFactorizationMonoid.irreducible_iff_prime); PID → Dedekind domain (inferInstance); prime ideals = maximal ideals in Dedekind domains (IsDedekindDomain.dimensionLtOne).
conclusion.implications: This proof places ℤ[√-5] within the broader landscape of algebraic number theory: it is a Dedekind domain with class number 2, the simplest example of a ring of algebraic integers that fails unique factorization. Dedekind's resolution — ideal unique factorization — is now the foundation of algebraic number theory, class field theory, and arithmetic geometry. The ideal class group Cl(K) for a number field K measures the 'distance' from unique element factorization; this proof formalizes the simplest non-trivial example. The machinery of Zsqrtd norms and the interval_cases strategy used here generalizes to other quadratic rings ℤ[√d], enabling systematic Lean verification of class number computations.
openQuestions: Can the ideal class group of ℤ[√-5] be proved to have order exactly 2 in Lean 4, formalizing the complete obstruction? Proving Cl(ℤ[√-5]) ≅ ℤ/2ℤ would require showing (2,1+√-5)² = (2) (principal) while (2,1+√-5) itself is not principal.

Can Mathlib's ideal FTA be applied concretely to ℤ[√-5] to write out the prime ideal factorization (6) = (2,1+√-5)²·(3,1+√-5)·(3,1-√-5), making the connection between element and ideal factorizations computationally tangible?

For which values of d does ℤ[√d] have class number 1 (i.e., is a UFD/PID), and can Lean verify these computationally? The Stark-Heegner theorem says there are exactly 9 such negative d: -1,-2,-3,-7,-11,-19,-43,-67,-163.
